title: Cloud economics
learningObjective: Explain fixed vs variable costs, on-premises cost components, licensing strategies, rightsizing, automation and economies of scale.
foundation: On-premises IT has big fixed costs: you buy servers, space, power and staff up front, whether you use them or not.
In AWS you mostly pay variable costs that rise and fall with use.
You save more by choosing the right size of resources (rightsizing), automating tasks, and benefiting from AWS's huge scale, which lowers prices.
engineer: Fixed vs variable: capital expenditure (CapEx) for hardware vs operational expenditure (OpEx) for consumption. Variable cost reduces waste from over-provisioning.
On-premises costs (total cost of ownership): servers, storage, network gear, data center space, power and cooling, software licences, hardware maintenance, refresh cycles and staff time.

Licensing: license-included (cost in the hourly price, for example Windows or SQL Server on EC2/RDS) vs Bring Your Own License (BYOL), which may require Dedicated Hosts for some licence terms; AWS License Manager tracks usage.
Rightsizing: match instance types and sizes to measured utilisation (AWS Compute Optimizer, Cost Explorer rightsizing recommendations).
Automation: IaC, scheduling start/stop, Auto Scaling and managed services reduce labour and errors.
Economies of scale: AWS's aggregated usage lowers per-unit costs, passed on as lower prices.

walkthrough.subtitle: Compare one year of running an app on-premises and on AWS and see where the money goes (illustrative numbers).

steps.label: Pay for peak
steps.title: You pay for the peak all year
body: Your app is busy two months a year. On-premises you must buy enough servers for that peak, and the servers sit mostly idle for the other ten months.
That money is spent up front, whether you use the capacity or not.

steps.label: Fixed vs variable
steps.title: Fixed costs vs variable costs
body: Fixed costs stay the same however much you use: servers you bought, a data center lease. Variable costs go up and down with use: pay-as-you-go cloud resources.
On AWS you run many servers in the busy months and few in the quiet ones, and the bill follows.

steps.label: Hidden costs
steps.title: On-premises costs more than the servers
body: The server price is only part of it. You also pay for power, cooling, floor space, physical security, network gear, hardware refreshes every few years, and the people who run all of it.
Compare total cost of ownership (TCO), not just the server price.

steps.label: Licensing
steps.title: Bring your own licence, or use one that's included
body: If you already own software licences (for example Windows Server or SQL Server), you may be able to bring them (BYOL), often on Dedicated Hosts. Otherwise choose licence-included instances, where the licence is part of the hourly price.
BYOL reuses what you have already paid for; licence-included is simpler and flexible.

steps.label: Rightsizing
steps.title: Rightsize: match the size to the load
body: Monitoring shows your servers running at 10% CPU. Rightsizing means switching to a smaller instance type, or fewer instances, that still meets the need.
On AWS that is a quick change, not a new hardware purchase.

steps.label: Automation
steps.title: Automate the routine work
body: Scripts and infrastructure as code start and stop environments on a schedule, deploy the same way every time, and replace manual steps.
Fewer manual hours and fewer mistakes both save money. Turning test servers off at night alone can cut their cost by more than half.

steps.label: Scale
steps.title: Economies of scale
body: AWS buys hardware and energy for a huge number of customers, which lowers its cost per unit. It has lowered prices many times as it grew.
You benefit without negotiating anything yourself.

steps.title: Where the savings come from
